fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give methanol. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 230 °C, 60 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Structured catalyst: space-time yield 0.74 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.25 bar, activity loss 7% after 100 h. Pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.36 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.37 bar, activity loss 12% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input:
The conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen into methanol is an important reaction, and the choice of catalyst plays a crucial role in determining how well it performs. In this study, two different catalyst forms are compared: a structured catalyst and a conventional pellet catalyst, both based on copper-zinc oxide. The reaction was carried out under well-defined conditions, namely a temperature of 230 °C, a pressure of 60 bar, and a feed ratio of H2/CO2 = 3, with a single feed composition being used throughout the work.

To evaluate the performance of the catalysts, the space-time yield was used as a key metric. The space-time yield is defined as the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour, expressed in kg L-1 h-1. In addition to the yield, the pressure drop across the catalyst and the loss of activity over time were also measured, providing a more complete picture of catalyst behaviour.

The results show that the structured catalyst performed considerably better than the pellet catalyst. The structured catalyst achieved a space-time yield of 0.74 kg L-1 h-1, whereas the pellet catalyst reached only 0.36 kg L-1 h-1, meaning that the structured form produced roughly twice as much methanol under the same conditions. The pressure drop was also much lower for the structured catalyst, at 0.25 bar, compared with 1.37 bar for the pellet catalyst. Furthermore, the structured catalyst proved to be more stable, losing 7% of its activity after 100 h, while the pellet catalyst lost 12% over the same period.

It is worth noting that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported together for the same catalyst charge, which makes this combined comparison particularly valuable. It should also be noted that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested in this work, so the behaviour of the catalysts in the presence of sulfur remains an open question for future investigation.
target:
Methanol is produced from carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst, and catalyst form changes the yield obtained from a given catalyst volume. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, so a comparison that reports both, for both forms, is missing. Two forms, structured and pellet, were compared at 230 °C and 60 bar with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and one feed composition. Space-time yield is defined as the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Pressure drop (bar) and activity loss after 100 h (%) were recorded for the same charges.

At these conditions the structured catalyst gave the higher space-time yield (0.74 kg L-1 h-1 against 0.36 kg L-1 h-1 for the pellet catalyst). Pressure drop was lower for the structured catalyst (0.25 bar against 1.37 bar). Activity loss after 100 h was also lower for the structured catalyst (7% against 12%). The three measures agree in direction: at the stated temperature, pressure and feed ratio, the structured form produced more methanol per unit catalyst volume per hour, at a lower pressure drop, with less activity lost over 100 h. Each figure is a single-charge figure at one feed composition, and the comparison holds at those conditions.

The comparison is limited to the conditions tested. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested, and catalyst behaviour with a sulfur-bearing feed is not reported. Activity is reported at 100 h and not beyond that time, and the feed composition was not varied. Within that scope, the structured catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.74 kg L-1 h-1 at a pressure drop of 0.25 bar with an activity loss of 7% after 100 h, against 0.36 kg L-1 h-1, 1.37 bar and 12% for the pellet catalyst.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% isopropanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 1.5 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 120, flux fell 15% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 0.9 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 560, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane, while vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as a vapour. In this study, two membranes were evaluated on a feed containing 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C, and their performance was compared using two key measures. The first measure is the flux, which is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour, expressed in kg m-2 h-1. The second measure is the separation factor, defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and it is a dimensionless quantity. Only one feed composition was tested in this work, and no test ran for longer than 500 h. The polymer membrane achieved a flux of 1.5 kg m-2 h-1 together with a separation factor of 120, although its flux fell by 15% over the course of 500 h. In contrast, the zeolite membrane showed a lower flux of 0.9 kg m-2 h-1 but a much higher separation factor of 560, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Overall, these results demonstrate a clear trade-off: the polymer membrane offers higher flux, and the zeolite membrane offers higher selectivity along with better stability. Interestingly, flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, which makes this direct comparison particularly valuable.
target: At 60 °C, on a feed of 85 wt% isopropanol in water, a zeolite membrane gave a separation factor of 560 with flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error, against 120 and a 15% fall in flux over 500 h for a polymer membrane. Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux (the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour, in kg m-2 h-1) was 1.5 kg m-2 h-1 for the polymer membrane and 0.9 kg m-2 h-1 for the zeolite membrane. Separation factor (the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, dimensionless) was 120 for the polymer membrane against 560 for the zeolite membrane. Stability over 500 h separated the two membranes in the same direction as the separation factor: polymer flux fell 15% over 500 h, and zeolite flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. One feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the three quantities are reported together here for both membranes at the one feed composition tested. Membrane choice at this feed composition rests on the quantity weighted most heavily: the polymer membrane carries the higher flux (1.5 against 0.9 kg m-2 h-1), and the zeolite membrane carries the higher separation factor (560 against 120) with flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 60 days at 13 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 90% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.2 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 2 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 60 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input:
Carbon capture from industrial sources such as cement kilns is widely seen as an important part of efforts to reduce carbon dioxide emissions. In this work, an amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas taken from a cement kiln, in order to see how the technology performs outside the laboratory.

The pilot unit was operated over a period of 60 days, treating gas at a rate corresponding to 13 t of carbon dioxide per day. Over this period, the unit captured 90% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas, which is an encouraging result for a pilot-scale system. The energy requirement of the process was also measured: the steam demand was 3.2 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured. In addition, the solvent loss was 2 kg per tonne captured, which is relevant to the operating cost of the process.

Overall, the results show that the unit could sustain a high capture rate over two months of operation while consuming steam and solvent at the levels reported above. However, some questions remain open. In particular, beyond 60 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested, so longer-term operation could still reveal problems that did not appear during the trial. Further work over longer periods would therefore be valuable to confirm that the performance seen here can be maintained.
target:
A pilot amine absorption unit treated gas from a cement kiln for 60 days at 13 t of carbon dioxide per day. The unit captured 90% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas over the 60 days. Steam demand was 3.2 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured. Solvent loss was 2 kg per tonne captured. Capture, steam demand and solvent loss are thus reported for the same unit over the same 60-day period, on cement kiln gas, at the stated rate.

The capture figure is an average over the treated gas of the whole period, at 13 t of carbon dioxide per day. Steam demand and solvent loss are stated per tonne captured, so the three figures share the captured tonne as the basis of the two demand figures and the period as the basis of the capture figure. No figure is reported for a period beyond 60 days, and no figure is reported at a second rate.

The tested scope ends at 60 days. Beyond 60 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested, and solvent behaviour under longer exposure to kiln dust is not reported. Within the tested period, the unit captured 90% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas at a steam demand of 3.2 gigajoules per tonne captured and a solvent loss of 2 kg per tonne captured.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.057 s-1. At 340 K, k = 2.858 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 83 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input: In this work, the rate constant of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two different temperatures in order to examine how the reaction rate changes with temperature. The rate constant, denoted by k and expressed in s-1, was determined at 300 K and at 340 K. At the lower temperature of 300 K, the value of k was found to be 0.057 s-1. At the higher temperature of 340 K, the value of k increased substantially to 2.858 s-1. It should be noted that the value at 340 K was not measured directly in the same way, but was instead computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 83 kJ mol-1, and it is therefore a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, which helps to ensure the reliability of the results, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%, indicating good reproducibility. It is also important to mention that no rate constant is reported above 340 K. This is because, above 340 K, the solvent evaporated during sampling, which made it impossible to obtain reliable measurements at higher temperatures. Taken together, these results clearly show that the rate constant increases significantly as the temperature rises from 300 K to 340 K, and they provide a useful basis for understanding the temperature dependence of this first-order reaction over the range that was studied.
target: Between 300 K and 340 K, the rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction rose from 0.057 s-1 to a derived 2.858 s-1. Rate constant k at 300 K was 0.057 s-1, measured directly. Rate constant k at 340 K was 2.858 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 83 kJ mol-1, and the 340 K value is a derived value rather than a direct measurement. Each temperature was measured in triplicate. Relative standard deviation of k was 4% across the triplicate measurements at each temperature. Sampling sets the upper limit of the reported range: above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, and no rate constant is reported above 340 K. Temperature dependence in the measured range is steep, with k at 340 K (2.858 s-1, derived) standing at about fifty times k at 300 K (0.057 s-1, measured). Precision of the underlying measurements is set by the triplicate design and the relative standard deviation of 4%. Reported values cover 300 K to 340 K only: a direct measurement at 300 K (0.057 s-1) and a derived value at 340 K (2.858 s-1, from the Arrhenius relation at activation energy 83 kJ mol-1), each measured in triplicate with a relative standard deviation of 4%, and no rate constant is reported above 340 K because the solvent evaporated during sampling above that temperature.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 218 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. At an adsorbent dose of 0.5 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 86% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: The adsorption of a dye from water onto activated carbon was investigated in a series of batch tests carried out at 298 K. The experimental data were fitted using the Langmuir model, and the fitted Langmuir capacity was found to be 218 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent. This capacity value was obtained at pH 6, and it is important to point out that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only, since the capacity at other pH values was not measured in this study. In addition to the capacity measurements, the removal performance of the activated carbon was also evaluated under specific operating conditions. At an adsorbent dose of 0.5 g L-1, the removal after 120 min reached 86% of the initial dye concentration. The initial dye concentration used in these tests was 50 mg L-1. Overall, these findings show that activated carbon is effective for removing the dye from water under the conditions that were tested, achieving a high level of removal within 120 min at a relatively low adsorbent dose. At the same time, the results should be interpreted with the scope of the study in mind, because the fitted capacity of 218 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent applies to pH 6, and no information is available from this work about how the capacity might change at other pH values, since those conditions were not measured. Further work would be needed to establish the capacity across a wider range of pH values. The batch tests therefore cover one temperature, 298 K, one initial dye concentration, 50 mg L-1, and the single reported pH value of 6 for the fitted capacity.
target: At pH 6, activated carbon gave a fitted Langmuir capacity of 218 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent in batch tests at 298 K, and removal reached 86% of an initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1 after 120 min at an adsorbent dose of 0.5 g L-1. Langmuir capacity (the fitted capacity in mg of dye per gram of adsorbent) was 218 mg g-1 at pH 6. Removal performance was measured at the same temperature: at an adsorbent dose of 0.5 g L-1, 86% of the initial dye concentration (50 mg L-1) was removed after 120 min. Batch conditions were held at 298 K across the tests. Reported capacity rests on the Langmuir fit at pH 6 only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured, and no capacity figure is reported for any pH other than 6. Removal is reported for one set of conditions: an initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, an adsorbent dose of 0.5 g L-1, and a contact time of 120 min, at 298 K. Dye removal on activated carbon at 298 K is characterised at pH 6 by a fitted Langmuir capacity of 218 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent and by 86% removal after 120 min at an adsorbent dose of 0.5 g L-1 from an initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, with capacity at other pH values unmeasured. Contact time in the removal test was 120 min, and the dose in that test was 0.5 g L-1. Temperature in both the capacity fit and the removal test was 298 K. Conditions beyond the reported set, including capacity at other pH values, were not measured.

fact_base: 180 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 947 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 44% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $392k installed, plus $66k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 23%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 23 pumps costs $38k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input:
This memo considers whether the plant should invest in maintenance sensors for its pumps, and it recommends a cautious first step. The plant operates 180 pumps, and maintenance records for the past 12 months show a total of 947 h of unplanned downtime, which is a significant burden on operations. Bearing failures are the single largest contributor, accounting for 44% of the downtime hours, and this makes the pumps a natural target for monitoring.

A sensor set covering all 180 pumps has been quoted at $392k installed, plus a further $66k per year. This is a substantial commitment, so the supporting evidence deserves careful attention. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 23%. However, it is important to bear in mind that this figure comes from the vendor and was not measured at this plant, so it may not transfer directly to our own conditions.

As a lower-cost alternative, a pilot on 23 pumps would cost $38k over three months. It should also be noted that spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. On balance, the memo recommends running the three-month pilot first. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and will report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation will be held until the pilot results have been reported.
target:
Recommendation: run a three-month pilot of maintenance sensors on 23 pumps at $38k before any decision on full installation. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.

The plant runs 180 pumps. Maintenance records for 12 months show 947 h of unplanned downtime, of which bearing failures account for 44% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $392k installed, plus $66k per year. A pilot on 23 pumps costs $38k over three months, against that full-installation quote.

Evidence for a benefit at this plant is indirect. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 23%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. No downtime reduction has been measured on any of the 180 pumps. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, so a pilot result would speak to downtime detection and not to spare-part supply.

Next step: the reliability engineering group runs the pilot on 23 pumps over three months and reports before the March capital review, at which the full-installation decision, on the quote of $392k installed plus $66k per year, is taken on pilot results.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 4 plants; revenue is $89 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 15392 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 85%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $2.6 million last year, up 27% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 2.9 weeks, against 1.7 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 63% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $333k; Plant 2 alone is $122k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.
input: This executive summary presents the delivery performance of a contract packaging firm that operates 4 plants and generates revenue of $89 million per year. The analysis is based on order records covering a period of 12 months, comprising a total of 15392 orders, which provides a comprehensive evidence base for the findings presented below. Over the last two quarters, the company's on-time delivery performance stood at 85%, which is significantly below the target of 95% that the company aims to achieve. At the same time, overtime cost reached $2.6 million last year, representing an increase of 27% on the year before, and the order backlog has grown to 2.9 weeks, compared with 1.7 weeks a year ago. A closer look at the data reveals that Plant 2 is the main source of the problem, accounting for 63% of all late orders across the company. In order to address this issue, a scheduling system has been considered, with a quoted cost of $333k for installation across all plants, or $122k for Plant 2 alone. An internal estimate, which is not a vendor figure, suggests that installing the system at Plant 2 could reduce overtime at that plant by 15-20% in the first year. Based on these findings, the recommendation under consideration is to install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first, while holding the other plants until the results from Plant 2 have been reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme and will be responsible for overseeing its implementation. In conclusion, the delivery problem is concentrated at Plant 2, and a phased installation beginning at that plant offers a targeted way to improve on-time delivery from its current level of 85% towards the target of 95%.
target: Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first, at a quoted $122k against $333k for all plants, and hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported; Plant 2 accounts for 63% of late orders, on order records for 12 months covering 15392 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 85% against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $2.6 million last year, up 27% on the year before. Backlog stands at 2.9 weeks, against 1.7 weeks a year ago. Late orders are concentrated in one plant of the four the firm runs: Plant 2 accounts for 63% of late orders, and revenue is $89 million per year across the 4 plants. Quoted cost of the scheduling system is $333k for all plants and $122k for Plant 2 alone. An internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. Trade-off in one line: Plant 2 installation costs $122k and addresses the plant carrying 63% of late orders, and the remaining plants stay on current scheduling until Plant 2 results are reported. Programme ownership sits with the operations director, who owns the scheduling programme. Sequencing limits the commitment to $122k of the $333k full installation while the plant with 63% of late orders is tested first. Evidence for the decision is the 12-month order record (15392 orders): on-time delivery of 85% against the 95% target, overtime of $2.6 million (up 27% on the year before), and a backlog of 2.9 weeks against 1.7 weeks a year ago. The recommendation under consideration covers Plant 2 only at this stage. Full installation across all plants, at the quoted $333k, is held until Plant 2 results are reported.

fact_base: A food plant uses 1871 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 11% of that use, a derived saving of 206 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $469k. At an electricity price of $0.1 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $21k and the derived simple payback is 22.3 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input: This executive summary considers a heat-recovery retrofit for a food plant, where refrigeration currently uses a substantial amount of electricity, amounting to 1871 MWh per year. According to a projection provided by the equipment vendor, the proposed retrofit could save 11% of that electricity use. This corresponds to a derived saving of 206 MWh per year, based on the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $469k, which is a significant investment for the plant. At an electricity price of $0.1 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out to $21k, and the derived simple payback period is 22.3 years, which is quite long. It is important to emphasise that the saving figure is a vendor projection and has not been measured at this plant, so there is some uncertainty around whether the projected savings will actually be achieved in practice. In addition, the refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, which is another limitation of the current analysis. In light of these considerations, the recommendation is to carry out a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is made. This trial approach will allow the actual savings to be measured before a major commitment is undertaken. The plant engineer owns the trial and will be responsible for reporting its results. The three refrigeration lines are therefore not all committed at once: one line carries the trial, and the remaining lines continue in their current form while the trial is carried out and its savings are measured.
target: Run a metered trial of the heat-recovery retrofit on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision; the vendor projection behind the full retrofit gives a derived simple payback of 22.3 years on a capital cost of $469k. Saving at the vendor figure is a derived 206 MWh per year. Annual saving at an electricity price of $0.1 per kWh is a derived $21k. Simple payback on the $469k capital cost is a derived 22.3 years. Status of the saving figure matters to the decision: the 11% saving is a vendor projection, and the saving was not measured at this plant. Trade-off in one line: a metered trial on one of three lines costs the trial only, and the $469k capital decision waits for a measured saving in place of a vendor projection with a derived payback of 22.3 years. Measured trial results will replace the vendor projection (11% of 1871 MWh per year) as the basis for the capital decision.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.025 m; mean velocity v = 2.1 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 52400 (computed as 998 x 2.1 x 0.025 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input:
In this worked example, we will calculate the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe and use it to determine the flow regime. The Reynolds number is a very important dimensionless quantity in fluid mechanics, and it is calculated from the density of the fluid, the mean velocity, the pipe diameter, and the dynamic viscosity, using the formula Re = rho v D / mu, where rho is the density (kg m-3), v is the mean velocity (m s-1), D is the pipe diameter (m), and mu is the dynamic viscosity (Pa s).

Let us now insert the values for water at 293 K. The density of the water is rho = 998 kg m-3, and its dynamic viscosity is mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter is D = 0.025 m, and the mean velocity of the flow is v = 2.1 m s-1.

Putting these numbers into the formula gives Re = 998 x 2.1 x 0.025 / 0.001, which works out to Re = 52400.

To interpret this result, we compare it with the usual thresholds. The flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000, while between these two values the regime is transitional and cannot be assigned by the number alone. Since our calculated value of 52400 is well above 4000, we can conclude that the flow in the pipe is turbulent.

Comparison of Re = 52400 with the thresholds puts the value above 4000. The Reynolds number for water in this pipe is 52400, and the flow regime at that number is turbulent.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick, so dC/dx = -500 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 1.05x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
In this example, we will work out the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film using Fick's first law. Fick's first law is a fundamental relationship in mass transfer, and it states that the diffusive flux J is given by J = -D dC/dx, where J is the diffusive flux (mol m-2 s-1), D is the diffusivity (m2 s-1), and dC/dx is the concentration gradient, with C being the concentration (mol m-3) and x the position (m). The negative sign in the equation is important, because it tells us that diffusion always runs from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration.

For oxygen in water, the diffusivity is D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. In our problem, the concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film that is 0.5 mm thick, so the concentration gradient works out to dC/dx = -500 mol m-4.

Now we can substitute these values into Fick's first law. This gives us J = -2.1 x 10-9 x (-500), which evaluates to J = 1.05 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The two negative signs cancel each other out, leaving a positive flux value.

To recap the steps of the calculation, we started from Fick's first law, inserted the diffusivity of oxygen in water, D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1, together with the concentration gradient of -500 mol m-4 that follows from the fall of 0.25 mol m-3 across the 0.5 mm film, and obtained the flux from the product of these quantities, with the sign of the result following from the two negative signs in the expression.

Finally, it is worth keeping in mind that the law in this form covers a stagnant medium. If the medium were moving, convection would also play a role in transporting the oxygen, and this extra contribution is not included in the equation used here. Within its range of validity, though, the calculation shows that the diffusive flux of oxygen through the film is 1.05 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1.
target:
Goal: calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film, from the stated diffusivity and concentration gradient. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is 1.05 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1 for oxygen in water with a diffusivity of 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1 and a concentration gradient of -500 mol m-4.

Fick's first law is J = -D dC/dx, where J denotes the diffusive flux (mol m-2 s-1), D denotes the diffusivity (m2 s-1), C denotes concentration (mol m-3) and x denotes position (m), so dC/dx is the change in concentration per unit distance (mol m-4). The negative sign in Fick's first law states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration: a concentration that falls as x increases gives a negative gradient and a positive flux in the direction of increasing x.

Inputs: oxygen in water has D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick, so dC/dx = -500 mol m-4. Substitution of D and dC/dx into J = -D dC/dx gives J = -(2.1 x 10-9) x (-500). Thus J = 1.05 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The sign of the result follows the sign convention of the law: the product of the stated negative sign and the negative gradient is positive.

Check: the computed flux has the sign the law requires for the stated gradient. Concentration falls across the film, the gradient dC/dx is negative, and Fick's first law returns a positive flux, in the direction from the higher concentration to the lower concentration. The magnitude of the flux rests on the two stated inputs only, the diffusivity of oxygen in water and the gradient across the 0.5 mm film, and no other quantity enters the calculation.

Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include, and the flux in a moving medium is not given by this calculation. The diffusive flux of oxygen through the stagnant water film, at the stated gradient, is 1.05 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 15.1 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input: The aim of this worked example is to calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction, and also to work out what fraction of the reactant remains after 60 min. For a first-order reaction, the half-life is related to the rate constant through a simple equation. The half-life, written as t1/2 and measured in min, is given by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, where k is the rate constant, measured in min-1. The fraction of reactant remaining after a time t, also measured in min, is given by the expression exp(-k t). In this example, the rate constant was measured as k = 0.046 min-1 at a temperature of 323 K. This value was obtained from concentration measurements that were taken every 5 min over a period of 90 min. Substituting the value of k into the half-life equation gives t1/2 = 15.1 min. Substituting k and t = 60 min into the fraction expression gives a fraction remaining of 0.06, which is a dimensionless quantity. It should be noted that these relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order would follow a different decay law, so the same equations should not be applied to reactions that are not first-order. Both of the calculated values, the half-life of 15.1 min and the fraction remaining of 0.06 after 60 min, rest on the single measured rate constant of 0.046 min-1 at 323 K and on the two relations given above for a first-order reaction.
target: For a first-order reaction with rate constant k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, the half-life is 15.1 min and the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06. Rate constant k (min-1) denotes the measured first-order rate constant, obtained from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min at 323 K, and its value in this example is 0.046 min-1. Half-life t1/2 (min) is defined by t1/2 = ln(2) / k for a first-order reaction. Substitution of k = 0.046 min-1 into the half-life relation thus gives t1/2 = 15.1 min. Fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t) for a first-order reaction. Substitution of k = 0.046 min-1 and t = 60 min thus gives exp(-0.046 x 60), a fraction remaining of 0.06 (dimensionless). A check on the two results uses the half-life itself: 60 min spans about four half-lives of 15.1 min, and four halvings leave about one sixteenth, or 0.06, of the starting amount, in agreement with the fraction computed from exp(-k t). The half-life relation and the fraction relation hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither relation applies to such a reaction. Measured input to both results is the one rate constant, k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min.

fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give dimethyl ether. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 250 °C, 50 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Washcoated monolith catalyst: space-time yield 0.94 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.24 bar, activity loss 8% after 100 h. Extruded pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.48 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.95 bar, activity loss 13% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input: In this study, carbon dioxide and hydrogen were reacted over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to produce dimethyl ether, and two different catalyst forms were compared under the same test conditions. The performance of the catalysts is described using the space-time yield, which is defined as the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour, expressed in kg L-1 h-1. All of the tests were carried out at 250 °C and 50 bar, with a feed ratio of H2/CO2 = 3, and only one feed composition was used throughout the work. The first catalyst was a washcoated monolith, which achieved a space-time yield of 0.94 kg L-1 h-1, with a pressure drop of 0.24 bar and an activity loss of 8% after 100 h. The second catalyst was an extruded pellet, which gave a lower space-time yield of 0.48 kg L-1 h-1, with a higher pressure drop of 0.95 bar and an activity loss of 13% after 100 h. Based on these results, the washcoated monolith performed better than the extruded pellet on all three of the measures reported here, delivering roughly twice the space-time yield at about a quarter of the pressure drop, together with a smaller loss of activity over the 100 h test period. It is important to note, however, that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested in this study, so the behaviour of these catalysts in the presence of sulfur remains unknown. It is also interesting to note that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which makes the combined reporting of both quantities in this work particularly useful for comparing the two catalyst forms. The comparison therefore rests on a single set of test conditions, namely 250 °C, 50 bar, a feed ratio of H2/CO2 = 3 and the one feed composition used for both catalyst forms, with each catalyst assessed over the same 100 h period for its activity loss.
target: At 250 °C and 50 bar, a washcoated monolith catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.94 kg L-1 h-1 at a pressure drop of 0.24 bar for dimethyl ether production from carbon dioxide and hydrogen, against 0.48 kg L-1 h-1 at 0.95 bar for an extruded pellet catalyst. Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give dimethyl ether. Space-time yield (the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour, in kg L-1 h-1) is reported for both catalyst forms at a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, with one feed composition tested. Washcoated monolith performance in full: space-time yield 0.94 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.24 bar, activity loss 8% after 100 h. Extruded pellet performance in full: space-time yield 0.48 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.95 bar, activity loss 13% after 100 h. Pressure drop separates the two forms by a factor of about four (0.24 against 0.95 bar), in the same direction as space-time yield (0.94 against 0.48 kg L-1 h-1). Activity loss after 100 h was lower for the monolith (8%) than for the pellet form (13%). Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge; both quantities are reported here for each charge, at 250 °C, 50 bar and a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested, and catalyst behaviour under a sulfur-bearing feed stands outside the reported results. At the one feed composition tested, the washcoated monolith gave the higher space-time yield (0.94 kg L-1 h-1), the lower pressure drop (0.24 bar) and the lower activity loss after 100 h (8%), against 0.48 kg L-1 h-1, 0.95 bar and 13% for the extruded pellet. Test duration for the activity figures was 100 h for both forms. Feed conditions were common to both forms throughout: 250 °C, 50 bar, a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, and the one feed composition tested.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% n-butanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 1.7 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 180, flux fell 14% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.1 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 560, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation process in which a liquid feed is placed in contact with one side of a membrane, and a vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane as a vapour. In the present study, two membranes were tested using a feed consisting of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at a temperature of 60 °C. The performance of the membranes was characterised by the flux, which is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour, in kg m-2 h-1, and by the separation factor, which is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless. Only one feed composition was tested, and no test was run for longer than 500 h. The polymer membrane produced a flux of 1.7 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 180, but its flux fell by 14% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane produced a flux of 1.1 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 560, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. These results show that the polymer membrane provides the higher flux, whereas the zeolite membrane provides the higher separation factor together with better stability. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, so reporting all three here is valuable.
target: On a feed of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C, a zeolite membrane gave a separation factor of 560 with flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error, and a polymer membrane gave a separation factor of 180 with flux falling 14% over 500 h. Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux (the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour, in kg m-2 h-1) was 1.7 kg m-2 h-1 for the polymer membrane and 1.1 kg m-2 h-1 for the zeolite membrane. Separation factor (the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, dimensionless) was 180 for the polymer membrane against 560 for the zeolite membrane. One feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. Stability over the 500 h test period followed the separation factor: polymer flux fell 14%, and zeolite flux was unchanged within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and all three are reported here for both membranes at the one feed composition tested. At this feed composition, the polymer membrane carries the higher flux (1.7 against 1.1 kg m-2 h-1), and the zeolite membrane carries the higher separation factor (560 against 180) with flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 45 days at 9 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.3 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 2.1 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas coming from a cement kiln, in order to evaluate its performance for capturing carbon dioxide under realistic operating conditions. The test programme ran for a period of 45 days, during which the unit treated gas at a rate corresponding to 9 t of carbon dioxide per day. Over this period, the unit captured 92% of the carbon dioxide present in the treated gas, which represents a high level of capture performance. The steam demand of the process was measured as 3.3 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and this figure represents an important part of the operating cost of the unit. The solvent loss was 2.1 kg per tonne of carbon dioxide captured. Taken together, these results indicate that the amine absorption unit operated effectively at pilot scale over the 45 days of testing, capturing the large majority of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas at the stated steam demand and solvent loss. However, it should be noted that the test programme lasted for 45 days only. Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested, so it is not known from this work how the solvent would be affected by kiln dust over longer periods of operation, or whether the capture performance would be maintained.
target: Over 45 days at 9 t of carbon dioxide per day, a pilot amine absorption unit on cement kiln gas captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas, at a steam demand of 3.3 gigajoules per tonne captured and a solvent loss of 2.1 kg per tonne captured. Capture is reported for the treated gas over the full test period: 92% of the carbon dioxide in that gas, at 9 t of carbon dioxide per day. Steam demand (3.3 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured) and solvent loss (2.1 kg per tonne captured) are reported on the same per-tonne basis. Test duration was 45 days at pilot scale. Kiln dust is the named gap in the test programme: beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. Reported performance therefore covers 45 days of operation, and solvent behaviour under kiln dust exposure beyond 45 days stands outside the reported results. Capture performance at pilot scale on cement kiln gas was 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas over 45 days at 9 t per day, with steam demand of 3.3 gigajoules per tonne captured and solvent loss of 2.1 kg per tonne captured, and the effect of kiln dust on the solvent beyond 45 days untested. Operating rate throughout the test was 9 t of carbon dioxide per day, on gas from a cement kiln, at pilot scale.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.042 s-1. At 340 K, k = 1.444 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 75 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input: In this study, the rate constant of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures, in order to investigate the effect of temperature on the reaction rate. The rate constant is denoted by k and is expressed in units of s-1. At a temperature of 300 K, the value of the rate constant was measured as k = 0.042 s-1. At a higher temperature of 340 K, the value of the rate constant was 1.444 s-1. It should be explained that this second value was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 75 kJ mol-1, and it is therefore a derived value rather than a directly measured one. Each of the temperatures was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was found to be 4%, which indicates that the measurements were reasonably consistent with one another. There is also an upper limit to the temperature range covered by this work. No rate constant is reported above 340 K, because above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, which prevented reliable measurements from being made at higher temperatures. In summary, the rate constant increased from 0.042 s-1 at 300 K to a derived value of 1.444 s-1 at 340 K, showing a strong dependence of the reaction rate on temperature over the range studied.
target: A first-order liquid-phase reaction gave a rate constant k (s-1) of 0.042 s-1 at 300 K and a derived 1.444 s-1 at 340 K. Rate constant k at 300 K was 0.042 s-1, measured directly. Rate constant k at 340 K was 1.444 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 75 kJ mol-1, and the 340 K value is a derived value rather than a direct measurement. Each temperature was measured in triplicate. Relative standard deviation of k was 4% across the triplicate measurements at each temperature. Sampling sets the upper limit of the reported range: above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, and no rate constant is reported above 340 K. Temperature dependence in the measured range is steep, with k at 340 K (1.444 s-1, derived) standing at about thirty-four times k at 300 K (0.042 s-1, measured). Precision of the underlying measurements is set by the triplicate design and the relative standard deviation of 4%. Reported values cover 300 K to 340 K only: a direct measurement at 300 K (0.042 s-1) and a derived value at 340 K (1.444 s-1, from the Arrhenius relation at activation energy 75 kJ mol-1), each measured in triplicate with a relative standard deviation of 4%, and no rate constant is reported above 340 K because the solvent evaporated during sampling above that temperature.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 248 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 88% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 7 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: The adsorption of a dye from water onto activated carbon was studied in batch tests carried out at a temperature of 298 K. The results were analysed using the Langmuir model, and the fitted Langmuir capacity was determined to be 248 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent. This capacity was obtained at pH 7, and it should be emphasised that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 7 only, because the capacity at other pH values was not measured during the course of this study. As well as determining the capacity, the study also measured how much of the dye could be removed under a particular set of conditions. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, the removal after 120 min was 88% of the initial dye concentration, which was 50 mg L-1 at the start of the test. These results demonstrate that activated carbon can remove a large proportion of the dye from water within 120 min under the conditions tested, and the fitted capacity of 248 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7 provides a measure of the maximum uptake indicated by the Langmuir model at that pH. Nevertheless, because capacity was not measured at other pH values, the findings of this study do not show how the capacity would change if the pH were different, and any application of the capacity figure should take this limitation into account. The removal figure of 88% and the capacity figure of 248 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent were both obtained at 298 K, the temperature at which all of the batch tests in this study were carried out.
target: Batch tests at 298 K gave activated carbon a fitted Langmuir capacity of 248 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7, with removal reaching 88% of an initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1 after 120 min at an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1. Langmuir capacity (the fitted capacity in mg of dye per gram of adsorbent) was 248 mg g-1 at pH 7. Removal performance was measured at the same temperature: at an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, 88% of the initial dye concentration (50 mg L-1) was removed after 120 min. Batch conditions were held at 298 K across the tests. Reported capacity rests on the Langmuir fit at pH 7 only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured, and no capacity figure is reported for any pH other than 7. Removal is reported for one set of conditions: an initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, and a contact time of 120 min, at 298 K. Dye removal on activated carbon at 298 K is characterised at pH 7 by a fitted Langmuir capacity of 248 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent and by 88% removal after 120 min at an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1 from an initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, with capacity at other pH values unmeasured. Contact time in the removal test was 120 min, and the dose in that test was 0.6 g L-1. Temperature in both the capacity fit and the removal test was 298 K. Conditions beyond the reported set, including capacity at other pH values, were not measured.

fact_base: 214 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1352 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 52% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 214 pumps is quoted at $462k installed, plus $69k per year. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input: This memo concerns the possible installation of maintenance sensors on the pumps at the plant, where a total of 214 pumps are currently in operation. According to the maintenance records covering a period of 12 months, the plant experienced 1352 h of unplanned downtime, which is a considerable amount of lost production time. Bearing failures are a major contributor to this problem, accounting for 52% of the downtime hours recorded. A sensor set covering all 214 pumps has been quoted at $462k installed, together with an ongoing cost of $69k per year. In a trial conducted by the vendor on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 20%; however, this figure is a vendor figure, and it was not measured at this plant. A more limited pilot, covering 18 pumps, would cost $34k over a period of three months. It should also be noted that spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. This memo therefore recommends the three-month pilot. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and will report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation will be held until the pilot results have been reported. The pilot covers 18 of the 214 pumps at the plant, over the three-month pilot period recommended in this memo.
target: Run the three-month pilot before any full installation: a pilot on 18 pumps costs $34k, against $462k installed plus $69k per year for a sensor set on all 214 pumps, and the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1352 h of unplanned downtime across the 214 pumps at the plant. Bearing failures account for 52% of the downtime hours. Downtime reduction claimed for the sensors is a vendor figure: in a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 20%, and the figure was not measured at this plant. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. Pilot ownership sits with the reliability engineering group, which owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review. Trade-off in one line: the pilot costs $34k over three months and tests the sensors on 18 pumps, and the full commitment of $462k plus $69k per year waits on measured results at this plant in place of the vendor figure of 20%. The pilot covers 18 pumps of the 214 at the plant. Reporting from the pilot goes to the March capital review, and the reliability engineering group reports before that review. Full installation covers all 214 pumps at the quoted figures if the decision is taken after the pilot results are reported.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 4 plants; revenue is $95 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 15415 orders. The order backlog stands at 4.1 weeks, against 1.8 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 59% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $277k; Plant 2 alone is $142k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.
input: This summary reviews the delivery performance of a contract packaging firm that operates 4 plants and generates revenue of $95 million per year. The analysis is based on order records covering 12 months and a total of 15415 orders, so the picture it gives is a broad one. Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery stood at 88%, which falls short of the target of 95% that the firm has set itself. At the same time, the costs of keeping up with demand have been rising: overtime cost $2.3 million last year, an increase of 28% on the year before. The order backlog has also grown considerably, and it now stands at 4.1 weeks, compared with 1.8 weeks a year ago. Looking at where the problem is concentrated, Plant 2 stands out, because it accounts for 59% of all late orders, well over half of the total. One option under consideration is a new scheduling system. A system covering all plants is quoted at $277k, while installing at Plant 2 alone would cost $142k. An internal estimate, which is not a vendor figure, suggests that overtime at Plant 2 could be reduced by 15-20% in the first year after installation. The recommendation under consideration is therefore to install the system at Plant 2 first and to hold the other plants until the results at Plant 2 have been reported and can be assessed. The operations director owns the scheduling programme and would oversee this work. In short, delivery performance is below target, costs are rising, the backlog is growing, and the lateness is concentrated mainly at a single plant, which is why a phased installation beginning at Plant 2 is the option being considered.
target: Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first and hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. On-time delivery is 88% over the last two quarters against a target of 95%, on order records for 12 months covering 15415 orders, and Plant 2 accounts for 59% of late orders. A contract packaging firm with 4 plants and revenue of $95 million per year is missing its delivery target while the cost of holding output rises. Backlog and overtime have both increased over the same period: the order backlog stands at 4.1 weeks, against 1.8 weeks a year ago, and overtime cost $2.3 million last year, up 28% on the year before. Plant 2 is the plant where late orders concentrate, at 59% of the total, and a phased installation puts the system where the late orders are. Quoted cost is $277k for a scheduling system at all plants and $142k at Plant 2 alone. An internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. Full installation is held, not cancelled: the decision on the remaining plants follows the Plant 2 results, and Plant 2 carries the larger part of the problem the system addresses. The operations director owns the scheduling programme. Installation at Plant 2 first costs $142k against $277k for all plants at once, and the difference between the two quoted costs stays uncommitted until measured results at Plant 2 support a wider installation. The remaining plants keep their present scheduling in the interval. Plant 2 results are reported before any further installation is approved.

fact_base: A food plant uses 1893 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 17% of that use, a derived saving of 322 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $312k. At an electricity price of $0.13 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $42k and the derived simple payback is 7.4 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input: This summary looks at a possible heat-recovery retrofit at a food plant, where refrigeration uses 1893 MWh of electricity per year. The equipment vendor projects that the retrofit would save 17% of that use, which works out to a saving of 322 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $312k. With electricity priced at $0.13 per kWh, the annual saving would be worth $42k, and the simple payback on the investment would be 7.4 years. It is important to note, however, that the saving figure is a vendor projection and has not been measured at this plant, so the 322 MWh per year and everything calculated from it rest on the vendor's estimate rather than on local data. There is also a gap in the analysis, because refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, and the peak month may behave differently from the year as a whole. Given these uncertainties, the recommendation is to carry out a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken. A trial of this kind would replace the projected saving with a measured one on a single line. The plant engineer owns the trial and would be responsible for running it and reporting what it finds.
target: Run a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision on the heat-recovery retrofit. Refrigeration at the food plant uses 1893 MWh of electricity per year, and the case for the retrofit rests on a vendor projection: a saving of 17% of that use, a derived saving of 322 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $312k, and at an electricity price of $0.13 per kWh the derived annual saving is $42k, with a derived simple payback of 7.4 years. Each of those figures is derived from the vendor projection, and the saving was not measured at this plant. Refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, and the annual figures carry no measurement from a peak month. A metered trial on one line measures the saving at this plant before $312k is committed. The trial replaces a projected saving with a measured saving on one of the three lines. The trial runs on one of the three lines, and the metered saving on that line is reported before the capital decision is taken.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. input: In this example we are going to calculate the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe, and then use the result to say what the flow regime is. The Reynolds number, Re, is a dimensionless quantity that is calculated from the density, the mean velocity, the pipe diameter and the dynamic viscosity using the formula Re = rho v D / mu, where rho is the density, v is the mean velocity, D is the pipe diameter and mu is the dynamic viscosity. The pipe in this example has a diameter of 0.08 m, and the water is flowing with a mean velocity of 0.9 m s-1. Substituting all of these values into the formula gives Re = 998 x 0.9 x 0.08 / 0.001, which works out to a Reynolds number of 71900. Now we need to interpret this result. The general rules are that the flow is laminar when the Reynolds number is below 2300, and it is turbulent when the Reynolds number is above 4000. In between these two values, that is, between 2300 and 4000, the flow is in a transitional regime, and in that range the regime is not assigned by the number alone. Since the value we have calculated, 71900, is much greater than 4000, we can conclude that the flow in this pipe is turbulent. It is worth noting that the Reynolds number itself has no units, because it is a ratio of quantities whose units cancel. In this case the comparison is straightforward, because the calculated value, 71900, does not lie anywhere near the transitional band between 2300 and 4000, and the density and viscosity used are the values for water at 293 K, with a pipe diameter of 0.08 m and a mean velocity of 0.9 m s-1.

input: This worked example calculates the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant film of water. The diffusive flux, J, which is measured in mol m-2 s-1, is obtained from the diffusivity D, measured in m2 s-1, together with the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is the concentration in mol m-3 and x is the position in m. The relationship used is Fick's first law, J = -D dC/dx. The negative sign in the equation is there because diffusion always runs from a region of high concentration towards a region of low concentration. For oxygen in water, the diffusivity is 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. In this example the concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across a film that is 0.8 mm thick, which means the concentration gradient is dC/dx = -250 mol m-4. Putting these numbers into Fick's first law gives J = 5.25x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1, which is the answer to the problem. Finally, it should be remembered that Fick's first law in the form given here applies to a stagnant medium. If the medium were moving, convection would also contribute to the transport of oxygen, and the equation as written does not include that contribution, so it would no longer tell the whole story. To recap the numbers used in the calculation, the diffusivity of oxygen in water is 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1, the concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across the 0.8 mm film, the gradient is -250 mol m-4, and the resulting flux is 5.25x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. input: In this example we will work out the half-life of a first-order reaction, and then find out what fraction of the reactant is still remaining after 60 minutes have passed. For a reaction that is first order, the half-life is directly connected to the rate constant through the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, where t1/2 is the half-life in minutes and k is the rate constant in min-1. In a similar way, the fraction of the reactant remaining after a time t is given by the exponential expression exp(-k t), which describes how the amount decreases as time goes on. The rate constant for the reaction considered here was measured as k = 0.069 min-1 at a temperature of 323 K. This value was obtained from concentration measurements that were taken every 5 min over a period of 90 min, so it is based on a whole series of measurements rather than on a single observation. Using the half-life relation, t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.069, which gives a half-life of 10 min. Using the fraction relation at t = 60 min, the fraction remaining is exp(-0.069 x 60), which comes out as 0.02, a dimensionless number meaning that only a small part of the original material is left after an hour. It is important to remember that these relations apply to a first-order reaction only. A reaction that follows a different order would decay in a different way and would be described by a different decay law, so the same formulas could not simply be carried across. The data behind the example are the measured rate constant of 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, taken from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min, and the two answers are a half-life of 10 min and a fraction remaining of 0.02 after 60 min.

input: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen can be reacted over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst in order to produce formaldehyde, and this study compares two different forms of the catalyst for this reaction. The performance measure used throughout is the space-time yield, which is defined as the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour, expressed in kg L-1 h-1. All of the tests were carried out at 280 °C and 40 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, and with a single feed composition. The first catalyst is a washcoated monolith, and it achieved a space-time yield of 1.09 kg L-1 h-1 with a pressure drop of only 0.1 bar, losing 8% of its activity after 100 h of operation. The second catalyst is an extruded pellet, and it gave a considerably lower space-time yield of 0.52 kg L-1 h-1, together with a much higher pressure drop of 1.4 bar, and it lost 19% of its activity after 100 h. It should be mentioned that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested in this work, so nothing can be said about how these catalysts would behave in the presence of sulfur. It is also interesting to note that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported together for the same catalyst charge in the literature, which makes a direct comparison of this kind relatively unusual. On the figures reported, the monolith gave the higher space-time yield, the lower pressure drop and the smaller activity loss of the two catalysts at 280 °C and 40 bar with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3.

input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is placed in contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum on the other side draws the component that permeates through the membrane as a vapour. Two measures are used to describe the performance of the membranes in this study. The first is the flux, which is the mass that permeates per unit membrane area per hour, in kg m-2 h-1. The second is the separation factor, defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, which is a dimensionless quantity. The feed used in the tests was 85 wt% n-butanol in water, and the tests were run at 60 °C. Only one feed composition was tested, and no test was allowed to run beyond 500 h. The polymer membrane produced a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 120, although its flux fell by 6% over the course of 500 h. The zeolite membrane produced a lower flux of 1 kg m-2 h-1, but its separation factor was much higher at 420, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. It is frequently the case that flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, so reporting all three together, as is done here, allows the two membranes to be compared across flux, selectivity and stability at the same time, with the polymer membrane offering the higher flux and the zeolite membrane offering the higher separation factor and the steadier performance over the full test duration of 500 h. In summary, the polymer membrane is the faster of the two membranes, and the zeolite membrane is the more selective and the more stable of the two over the 500 h for which it was tested at 60 °C.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. input: An amine absorption unit has been tested at pilot scale on gas coming from a cement kiln, and this passage reports how the unit performed during the test campaign. The campaign lasted for 45 days, and during that time the unit treated gas at a rate corresponding to 13 t of carbon dioxide per day. Over the campaign, the unit succeeded in capturing 86% of the carbon dioxide that was present in the treated gas, so the large majority of the carbon dioxide entering the unit was removed from the gas stream. The energy requirement of the process was recorded as a steam demand of 3.9 gigajoules for every tonne of carbon dioxide captured, which makes steam the figure to watch when the operating cost of the unit is considered. Solvent was also consumed during operation, and the solvent loss amounted to 2.1 kg per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, so the solvent has to be made up continuously as the unit runs. These three results, the capture rate of 86%, the steam demand of 3.9 gigajoules per tonne captured and the solvent loss of 2.1 kg per tonne captured, describe the performance of the unit at the tested throughput of 13 t of carbon dioxide per day over the full 45 days of the campaign. One question remains open at the end of the work. Beyond 45 days, the effect that kiln dust has on the solvent is untested, because the campaign did not run for longer than 45 days, and so it is not yet known how the solvent would be affected by kiln dust over a longer period of operation on cement kiln gas. The campaign therefore gives a complete set of performance figures for the 45 days it covers, at 13 t of carbon dioxide per day, and no figures at all for any longer period of operation on the kiln gas.

input: The rate constant, k, of a first-order reaction taking place in the liquid phase was measured at two different temperatures, and the results of those measurements are reported here. input: The adsorption of a dye from water onto a metal-organic framework was studied in a series of batch tests, all of which were carried out at a temperature of 298 K. In other words, the study reports how much dye this adsorbent can hold at pH 6, namely 148 mg per gram, and how much dye was removed in 120 min at a dose of 0.8 g L-1, namely 83% of the starting 50 mg L-1, at 298 K.

input: This memo concerns the possible installation of maintenance sensors on the pumps at the plant, where 180 pumps are in operation. A smaller first step is available in the form of a pilot on 19 pumps, which would cost $39k spread over three months. It is also worth recording that spare-part lead times are not changed by the sensors, so that side of the maintenance picture would remain as it is. This memo therefore recommends the three-month pilot. fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. input:
In this worked example, we are going to compute the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe and then state what flow regime it corresponds to. The Reynolds number, Re, is dimensionless, and it is computed from the density rho, the mean velocity v, the pipe diameter D and the dynamic viscosity mu using the relation Re = rho v D / mu. Here rho is in kg m-3, v is in m s-1, D is in m and mu is in Pa s. For water at 293 K, the density is 998 kg m-3 and the dynamic viscosity is 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter is 0.05 m and the mean velocity is 2.3 m s-1. Putting these values into the equation gives Re = 998 x 2.3 x 0.05 / 0.001, which works out to a value of 114800. So the Reynolds number for this case is 114800. In general, flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000. Between these two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. Since 114800 is well above 4000, the flow in this example falls on the turbulent side of the stated thresholds. It is worth noting that the result depends on all four quantities in the relation, namely the density, the velocity, the diameter and the viscosity, and changing any of them would change the Reynolds number obtained. The calculation therefore uses the water properties at 293 K given above, together with the stated pipe diameter of 0.05 m and the stated mean velocity of 2.3 m s-1, to give the final dimensionless result of 114800 for this pipe flow case.
 To summarise the inputs once more, the density is 998 kg m-3, the viscosity is 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s, the diameter is 0.05 m and the velocity is 2.3 m s-1.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across a film 0.8 mm thick, so dC/dx = -250 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 6.50x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. In this worked example, the goal is to compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film using Fick's first law. The diffusive flux J, expressed in mol m-2 s-1, is computed from the diffusivity D, in m2 s-1, and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is the concentration in mol m-3 and x is position in m. Fick's first law is written as J = -D dC/dx, and the negative sign in the equation indicates that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. For oxygen in water, the diffusivity D is 2.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. In the film considered here, the concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across a film that is 0.8 mm thick, so the concentration gradient dC/dx is -250 mol m-4. Substituting these values into Fick's first law gives J = 6.50x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. This is the worked result for the diffusive flux of oxygen through the film. It should be noted that the law as stated covers a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include, so the calculation applies to the stagnant case only. To recap the main numbers used in the example, the diffusivity is 2.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1, the concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across a film 0.8 mm thick, the gradient is -250 mol m-4, and the resulting flux is 6.50x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The example therefore shows how the flux follows directly from the diffusivity and the concentration gradient once those two quantities are known for the film.
 The film thickness matters to the result because the gradient is the fall in concentration divided over that thickness: a fall of 0.2 mol m-3 over 0.8 mm gives the gradient of -250 mol m-4 used above, and a different thickness would give a different gradient and therefore a different flux from the same law.

It is also worth noting that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which makes a combined comparison of this kind less common in the literature. Overall, the comparison is based on the tests at 230 °C and 60 bar with the single feed composition described above, and the results reported here are the space-time yield, the pressure drop and the activity loss after 100 h for each of the two catalyst forms tested.
