The record stands on one basis for both forms. Temperature was 280 °C, pressure was 40 bar, and the feed ratio H2/CO2 was 3 in each test, at the one feed composition used. The structured value of 0.71 kg L-1 h-1 and the pellet value of 0.35 kg L-1 h-1 are space-time yields at those conditions, and the pressure drops and activity losses stand in the same record.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% isopropanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 1.9 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 120, flux fell 12% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.2 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 560, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input:
Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is placed in contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane as a vapour. In this study, two membrane types were compared for the separation of isopropanol and water, using a feed containing 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C. Two key performance measures were used throughout the work. Flux is defined as the mass of material permeating per unit membrane area per hour, expressed in kg m-2 h-1, while the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless.

The polymer membrane achieved a flux of 1.9 kg m-2 h-1, which was higher than the flux of 1.2 kg m-2 h-1 obtained with the zeolite membrane. However, the zeolite membrane gave a much higher separation factor of 560, compared with a value of only 120 for the polymer membrane, showing a clear trade-off between flux and selectivity in the results. In terms of stability, the flux of the polymer membrane fell by 12% over 500 h of operation, whereas the flux of the zeolite membrane remained unchanged over the same period, within measurement error.

It is important to note that only one feed composition was tested in this work, and no test was run for longer than 500 h, so the longer-term behaviour of both membranes remains unknown. Overall, the results show that the polymer membrane offers higher throughput, while the zeolite membrane offers better separation and better stability. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and reporting all three here helps to give a more complete picture of how the two membrane types compare in practice for this particular separation task.
target:
Pervaporation separates a liquid mixture by contact with one side of a membrane; vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Two membranes were compared on one feed (85 wt% isopropanol in water, at 60 °C), and flux, selectivity and stability are reported together for the same membrane, a combination seldom reported. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). Separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless).

Polymer gave the higher flux (1.9 kg m-2 h-1, against 1.2 kg m-2 h-1 for zeolite). Zeolite gave the higher separation factor (560, against 120 for polymer). Higher flux and higher selectivity therefore sit in different membranes, and a choice between the two rests on which quantity governs the separation duty. Stability separates the pair in the same direction as selectivity: polymer flux fell 12% over 500 h, while zeolite flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. A membrane selected for throughput carries a measured flux loss over the test period; a membrane selected for separation factor carries none within measurement error.

One feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. At that feed and over that period, zeolite holds the higher separation factor (560) and unchanged flux, while polymer holds the higher flux (1.9 kg m-2 h-1) with a 12% loss over 500 h. Behaviour at other feed compositions, and beyond 500 h for either membrane, is outside the tested record.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 45 days at 9 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 88% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.2 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 2 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input:
An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln in order to evaluate its performance for carbon dioxide capture under realistic operating conditions. The pilot campaign was carried out over a period of 45 days, during which the unit treated gas at a rate corresponding to 9 t of carbon dioxide per day. During the campaign, the unit captured 88% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas, which represents a strong level of performance for a pilot-scale system of this kind, and this capture level is the main headline result of the work.

The energy demand of the process was also measured. The steam demand was found to be 3.2 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and the solvent loss was 2 kg per tonne of carbon dioxide captured. These figures are important because steam demand and solvent loss are two of the main operating costs associated with amine-based capture, and they help to determine whether the process can be economically attractive at a larger scale.

It should be noted, however, that the campaign lasted only 45 days. Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested, and so it is not yet known how the solvent will behave over longer periods of operation on cement kiln gas. Further work over a longer period would therefore be needed in order to confirm the durability of the solvent and the stability of the capture performance reported here, and to establish whether the steam demand and solvent loss remain at the levels measured during this 45-day campaign.
target:
Over 45 days on cement kiln gas at 9 t of carbon dioxide per day, a pilot amine absorption unit captured 88% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.2 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 2 kg per tonne captured. Capture, steam demand and solvent loss are reported for the same 45-day campaign, so the three figures describe one operating period at one throughput.

Kiln gas is the feed throughout the campaign, and the unit is an amine absorption unit at pilot scale. Capture, steam demand and solvent loss each refer to the carbon dioxide in that treated gas, at the campaign rate, over the full 45 days of the test.

Steam demand sets the energy cost of the capture at the measured rate: each tonne captured carries 3.2 gigajoules of steam over the campaign. Solvent loss sets the make-up cost on the same basis, at 2 kg for each tonne captured across the 45 days. Both figures rest on the treated gas rate of 9 t of carbon dioxide per day, and both are averages over the campaign rather than values from a single day. Capture at 88% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas was held over the same period in which those two consumption figures were recorded.

Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. The tested record is a 45-day campaign at 9 t of carbon dioxide per day, with capture at 88%, steam demand at 3.2 gigajoules per tonne captured and solvent loss at 2 kg per tonne captured. Solvent behaviour under kiln dust exposure past 45 days, and capture performance past that point, are outside the tested record.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.024 s-1. At 340 K, k = 0.622 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 69 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input:
The rate constant of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two different temperatures in this study, in order to characterise how the reaction rate depends on temperature. At the lower temperature of 300 K, the rate constant k was measured as 0.024 s-1. At the higher temperature of 340 K, the value of k was considerably larger, at 0.622 s-1. This second value was not measured directly, but was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 69 kJ mol-1, and it is therefore a derived value rather than a direct measurement, a distinction that should be kept in mind when the two values are compared.

Each temperature was measured in triplicate, which means that three separate measurements were made under the same conditions, and the relative standard deviation of the rate constant was found to be 4%, indicating that the measurements were reasonably consistent with one another. The increase in the rate constant between 300 K and 340 K is substantial, rising by more than an order of magnitude across a temperature interval of only 40 K, which is consistent with the relatively high activation energy used in the Arrhenius calculation, and shows the strong sensitivity of this reaction to temperature changes.

The triplicate measurements were made at each of the two temperatures studied, 300 K and 340 K, and the same relative standard deviation of 4% applies to the rate constant values reported for this first-order liquid-phase reaction at both of those temperatures.

It is also important to note the upper limit of the measurements. Above 340 K, the solvent evaporated during sampling, which made it impossible to obtain reliable samples, and so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. As a result, the temperature dependence of the reaction is only characterised up to 340 K in this work, and any behaviour at higher temperatures remains unreported and would require a different sampling approach to be studied properly.
target:
Between 300 K and 340 K, the rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction rises from 0.024 s-1 to 0.622 s-1. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. The two values differ in standing: the value at 300 K is a measurement, and the value at 340 K is a derived value, computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 69 kJ mol-1.

Triplicate measurement fixes the spread behind each reported value, at a relative standard deviation of 4% for k at both temperatures. A change in temperature of 40 K carries the stated increase in k, from 0.024 s-1 at 300 K to 0.622 s-1 at 340 K. Comparison between the endpoints rests on unlike bases, one measured and one derived, and the reported spread of 4% belongs to the measurements made in triplicate at each temperature.

The reaction is liquid-phase and first-order, and k is reported in s-1 at both temperatures. Measurement in triplicate at 300 K and at 340 K gives the same relative standard deviation, 4%, at each temperature. The Arrhenius relation supplies the 340 K value from an activation energy of 69 kJ mol-1, and that derived standing stays attached to the value wherever the pair of endpoints is reported together as a comparison.

Above 340 K, the solvent evaporated during sampling, and no rate constant is reported above 340 K. Within the reported range, k is 0.024 s-1 at 300 K by measurement, and 0.622 s-1 at 340 K as a derived value from the Arrhenius relation at an activation energy of 69 kJ mol-1, with a relative standard deviation of 4% on the triplicate measurements. Rate behaviour past 340 K is outside the reported record, because sampling failed there through solvent evaporation.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 185 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7. At an adsorbent dose of 1.1 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 85% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 7 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input:
The adsorption of a dye from water onto a metal-organic framework was investigated in a series of batch tests carried out at 298 K. The experimental data were fitted using the Langmuir model, and the fitted Langmuir capacity of the adsorbent was found to be 185 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7, which represents the maximum capacity obtained from the fit under the conditions studied. Tests were also carried out at an adsorbent dose of 1.1 g L-1, starting from an initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. After 120 min of contact, the removal achieved under these conditions was 85% of the initial dye concentration.

It is important to note that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 7 only, as this was the pH value used in the tests described here. The capacity of the metal-organic framework at other pH values was not measured in this study, and so no conclusions can be drawn about how the adsorption performance might change if the pH of the water were higher or lower than 7. Overall, the results show that the material can remove a large proportion of the dye from water within 120 min at the dose tested, and that it has a fitted capacity of 185 mg per gram at pH 7 and 298 K in these batch tests.
target:
At 298 K in batch tests, a metal-organic framework adsorbed dye from water with a fitted Langmuir capacity of 185 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7. Removal after 120 min was 85% of the initial dye concentration (50 mg L-1) at an adsorbent dose of 1.1 g L-1. Capacity and removal are reported for the same test series, at one temperature (298 K) and one pH (pH 7). Batch tests at 298 K are the setting for both figures, and the reported capacity and the reported removal both belong to that setting and to no other.

Langmuir capacity is a fitted quantity: 185 mg per gram comes from the Langmuir fit to the batch data, at pH 7. Removal is a measured outcome at a stated dose and contact time, 85% after 120 min at 1.1 g L-1 from an initial concentration of 50 mg L-1. Dose, contact time and initial concentration fix the removal figure; a different dose or a different contact time is a different test, outside the reported set.

The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 7 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured. At pH 7 and 298 K, the fitted capacity is 185 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent, and removal at a dose of 1.1 g L-1 reached 85% of the initial dye concentration after 120 min. Capacity at any other pH is outside the measured record.

fact_base: 214 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 968 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 50% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 214 pumps is quoted at $439k installed, plus $76k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 26%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 22 pumps costs $40k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. input:
This memo considers the case for installing a sensor set on the pumps at the plant, where a total of 214 pumps are currently in operation. Maintenance records covering a period of 12 months show a total of 968 h of unplanned downtime, which is a significant burden on the plant. Bearing failures are the largest single contributor to this problem, accounting for 50% of the downtime hours recorded over the 12-month period, and it is this category of failures that the proposed sensors are mainly intended to address.

A sensor set covering all 214 pumps has been quoted at $439k installed, with an additional ongoing cost of $76k per year. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 26%, although it should be noted that this figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant, so it may not be reproduced here. It should also be noted that spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors.

Rather than committing to the full installation at this stage, this memo recommends a three-month pilot on 22 pumps, at a cost of $40k. The reliability engineering group will own the pilot and will report its results before the March capital review. The decision on full installation will be held until the pilot results have been reported, so that the decision can be based on evidence gathered at this plant.
target:
Recommendation: run a three-month pilot on 22 pumps at $40k, and hold the decision on full installation until the pilot results are reported. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review.

Unplanned downtime stands at 968 h over 12 months of maintenance records across 214 pumps, and bearing failures account for 50% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 214 pumps is quoted at $439k installed, plus $76k per year. Against that cost stands a vendor figure: in a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 26%. The 26% figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant, and spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors.

A pilot converts the vendor figure into a plant measurement at $40k, against a full-installation commitment of $439k installed plus $76k per year. The pilot covers 22 of the 214 pumps over three months, under the reliability engineering group, with reporting before the March capital review. input:
This executive summary presents an overview of delivery performance at a contract packaging firm that operates 4 plants and has revenue of $112 million per year. The analysis is based on order records covering a period of 12 months, comprising a total of 16892 orders. Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery has been running at 90%, which is below the target level of 95% that the firm has set for itself. Overtime cost was $2.4 million last year, which was up 29% on the year before, and the order backlog currently stands at 4.1 weeks, compared with 2 weeks a year ago, indicating that the delivery problem has been getting worse rather than better over the period covered by the records.

A closer look at the data shows that Plant 2 accounts for 67% of all late orders, which makes it the clear focus of the problem. A new scheduling system has been quoted at $317k for all plants, or at $126k for Plant 2 alone. An internal estimate suggests that installing the system at Plant 2 could reduce overtime there by 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration is therefore to install the system at Plant 2 first, and to hold the other plants until the results from Plant 2 have been reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.

fact_base: A food plant uses 2452 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. At an electricity price of $0.13 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $41k and the derived simple payback is 12.1 years. input:
This executive summary looks at a proposed heat-recovery retrofit at a food plant, where refrigeration currently uses 2452 MWh of electricity per year. According to projections provided by the equipment vendor, the retrofit would save 13% of that electricity use, which works out at a derived saving of 319 MWh per year based on the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $496k. Using an electricity price of $0.13 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $41k, and the derived simple payback on the investment is 12.1 years, which is a long payback period for a project of this kind.

It is important to emphasise that the saving figure behind these calculations is a vendor projection, and it was not measured at this plant, so the actual saving achieved in practice could be different from the figure used here. It should also be noted that the refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, and the peak month could have an important effect on the results. For these reasons, the recommendation is that a metered trial should be carried out on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken on the retrofit. The plant engineer will own the trial, and the trial will provide measured data from the plant itself to replace the vendor projection on which the current figures are based. The metered trial is therefore the recommended next step before any commitment of the $496k capital cost is made by the plant.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.08 m; mean velocity v = 1 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 79800 (computed as 998 x 1 x 0.08 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input:
In this worked example, the goal is to calculate the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe, and then to use the result to state the flow regime. The Reynolds number is an important dimensionless quantity in fluid mechanics, and it is calculated from the density of the fluid, the mean velocity, the pipe diameter and the dynamic viscosity using the formula Re = rho v D / mu, where rho is the density in kg m-3, v is the mean velocity in m s-1, D is the pipe diameter in m, and mu is the dynamic viscosity in Pa s.

For water at 293 K, the density is 998 kg m-3 and the dynamic viscosity is 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter in this example is 0.08 m, and the mean velocity of the water is 1 m s-1. Substituting these values into the formula gives Re = 998 x 1 x 0.08 / 0.001, which works out to give a Reynolds number of 79800.

To interpret this result, the Reynolds number is compared with the standard threshold values. The flow is laminar when the Reynolds number is below 2300, and it is turbulent when the Reynolds number is above 4000. Between these two values, the flow is in a transitional regime, which is not assigned by the number alone. Since the calculated value of 79800 is well above 4000, the flow of water in this pipe is turbulent. The values used in the calculation are the values given for this example, namely water at 293 K, flowing in the stated pipe of 0.08 m diameter, at the stated mean velocity of 1 m s-1.
target:
Calculate the Reynolds number for water in a pipe, and state the flow regime. The result is Re = 79800 (dimensionless), and the flow is turbulent.

The Reynolds number Re is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K has rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter is D = 0.08 m, and mean velocity is v = 1 m s-1. Each input belongs to the same flow: one fluid, at one temperature, in one pipe, at one mean velocity.

Substitution of the stated values gives Re = 998 x 1 x 0.08 / 0.001. Thus Re = 79800, from the density, velocity and diameter in the numerator and the viscosity in the denominator of the stated relation. A change in any one input changes the result through that relation: diameter and velocity enter in proportion, and viscosity enters in inverse proportion, at the stated values of the remaining inputs.

Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. Comparison of the computed value with the two thresholds places 79800 above the turbulent threshold, by a wide margin over 4000 and far from the transitional band. Water in a pipe of diameter 0.08 m at a mean velocity of 1 m s-1 and 293 K is in turbulent flow, at Re = 79800.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.8 mm thick, so dC/dx = -312 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 5.00x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
The goal of this worked example is to calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant film of water, using Fick's first law. The diffusive flux J, which has units of mol m-2 s-1, depends on the diffusivity D, in m2 s-1, and on the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is the concentration in mol m-3 and x is the position in m. Fick's first law is written as J = -D dC/dx. The negative sign in the equation is there because diffusion takes place from a region of high concentration towards a region of low concentration.

For oxygen in water, the diffusivity is 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Across the water film, which is 0.8 mm thick, the concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3, so the concentration gradient is dC/dx = -312 mol m-4. Substituting these values into Fick's first law gives J = 5.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1, which is the diffusive flux of oxygen through the film.

The calculation uses the diffusivity for oxygen in water given above, together with the concentration fall of 0.25 mol m-3 across the 0.8 mm film given above, and no other data.

It should be remembered that Fick's first law, as it is stated here, applies to a stagnant medium. If the medium were moving, convection would also contribute to the transport of oxygen, and this effect is not included in the equation used in this example.
target:
Calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The result is J = 5.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1, directed from high concentration to low concentration.

The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C denotes concentration (mol m-3) and x denotes position (m). Fick's first law is J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water has D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.8 mm thick, so dC/dx = -312 mol m-4.

Substitution gives J = -(1.6 x 10-9) x (-312). Thus J = 5.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The two negative signs, one in the law and one in the gradient, give a positive flux in the direction from high concentration to low concentration, as the sign convention in Fick's first law requires.

Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include. The flux of 5.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1 is the diffusive flux through the stagnant film alone, at the stated diffusivity and the stated concentration fall across 0.8 mm, and no convection term enters the stated result.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 15.1 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input:
The aim of this worked example is to calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction, and then to find the fraction of the reactant that remains after 60 min.
